title: Creative Writing
description: Developing your voice as a writer — generating ideas, crafting settings and characters, using sensory detail, editing, and finding inspiration.

notes.heading: Generating Ideas
notes.body: Writer's block happens to everyone — having strategies helps. Techniques: Freewriting (write continuously without stopping or editing for 5-10 minutes), Prompts (a sentence, image, word, or scenario to start from), 'What if?' (take an ordinary situation and change one element), Observation (eavesdrop, people-watch, notice details), Memory mining (your own experiences are rich material — not autobiography, but emotional truth), Constraints (limit yourself — 100 words, one-syllable words only, no adjectives — constraints spark creativity). The most important rule of generating ideas: don't judge while generating. First drafts are for getting ideas down. Editing and judgment come later. Quantity leads to quality — write more, and the good ideas will emerge.

illustration.alt: Diagram of a glowing lightbulb surrounded by six labelled idea-generation techniques: freewriting, prompts, asking 'what if?', observation, memory mining, and constraints.
illustration.caption: Six reliable strategies for generating ideas — generate freely first and save judgement for the editing stage.

notes.heading: Show, Don't Tell
notes.body: The golden rule of creative writing. 'Tell': 'She was angry.' 'Show': 'Her jaw tightened. Her knuckles whitened around the phone. When she spoke, each word came out clipped and cold, like ice chips.' Showing creates immersion — the reader experiences the emotion rather than being told about it. To show: use sensory details, actions, dialogue, internal physical sensations. Avoid abstract labels for emotions ('sad,' 'happy,' 'angry') — describe what that emotion looks and feels like in the body and behaviour. However: 'tell' has its place. Use it for transitions, background information, and when showing would slow pacing unnecessarily. Skillful writers know when to show and when to tell.

notes.heading: Crafting Setting and Atmosphere
notes.body: Setting is not background — it actively shapes story. Create world through: Sensory details (not just sight — sounds, smells, textures, temperature), Specificity ('a 1972 mustard-yellow Ford pickup with a dented tailgate' > 'an old car'), Weather and light (establish mood and time), Contrast (beauty amidst decay, silence within chaos). Atmosphere: the emotional tone of a scene, created through word choice, pacing, and sensory detail. Gothic: darkness, decay, isolation, the uncanny. Dystopian: greyness, surveillance, uniformity, oppression. Magical realism: the extraordinary treated as ordinary. Use pathetic fallacy thoughtfully — it can feel heavy-handed if overused ('rain at a funeral' is cliché — subvert expectations).

notes.heading: Dialogue That Works
notes.body: Good dialogue: advances plot, reveals character, creates tension, and sounds natural (but is more purposeful than real speech). Tips: Each character should sound different — vocabulary, sentence length, rhythm, what they notice. Read dialogue aloud — if it sounds awkward, rewrite. Avoid 'talking heads' — anchor dialogue in physical action and setting. Subtext: what characters DON'T say is often more important than what they do. 'I'm fine' = probably not fine. Dialogue tags: 'said' is usually best (invisible). Avoid overusing alternatives ('exclaimed,' 'retorted,' 'opined'). Use action beats instead of tags: 'He slammed his mug on the table. 'I'm not going back there.''

notes.heading: Openings: Hooking the Reader
notes.body: The first sentence is your one chance to grab attention. Effective openings: Start in the middle of action (in medias res). Create mystery or a question the reader wants answered. Establish a distinctive voice immediately. Present something unexpected or contradictory. Use a striking image or sensory detail. Openings to avoid: waking up, weather reports, looking in a mirror and describing appearance, 'It was a dark and stormy night,' excessive backstory before anything happens. The first paragraph is a promise to the reader about what kind of story this will be — fulfil that promise.

notes.heading: Writing with Sensory Detail
notes.body: Engage all five senses — not just sight. Sound: the creak of floorboards, distant traffic, silence itself. Smell: the most memory-linked sense — freshly cut grass, stale cigarette smoke, ocean salt. Touch: texture, temperature, pressure — the roughness of brick, the chill of metal. Taste: not just food — the metallic taste of fear, dust in the air. Synaesthesia: mixing senses ('the colour of her voice,' 'the sharp smell of ozone'). The best sensory details are specific and unexpected. Not 'it smelled bad' but 'it smelled like wet dog and burnt toast.' Not 'the room was cold' but 'her breath misted in the air, and the floorboards stung her bare feet.'

notes.heading: Editing and Revising
notes.body: Writing is rewriting. First draft: get it down. Second draft: fix big problems — structure, character, pacing, voice. Third draft: line edits — sentence flow, word choice, dialogue. Final draft: proofreading. Edit checklist: (1) Does your opening hook readers? (2) Does every scene earn its place? (3) Are your characters distinct and consistent? (4) Have you shown rather than told where it matters? (5) Can you cut 10% of your words? (6) Have you varied sentence length and structure? (7) Is the ending satisfying — does it resonate? Read aloud — your ear catches what your eye misses. Distance helps: put the draft away for a day before editing. Give yourself permission to write badly first — you can fix a bad page, but you can't fix a blank one.

flashcards.definition: Describe sensory details and actions so readers experience emotions rather than being told about them.
flashcards.example: Tell: 'He was nervous.' Show: 'His hands trembled. He wiped his palms on his jeans for the third time.'

flashcards.definition: Writing continuously without stopping or editing for a set time — silences the inner critic.
flashcards.example: Set timer for 5 minutes. Write without lifting pen. Don't edit, don't judge — just generate.

flashcards.definition: Starting in the middle of action — plunging readers directly into a scene.
flashcards.example: 'The gun was in her hand before she heard the door open.' — immediate tension, no setup.

flashcards.definition: What characters mean but don't say — the unspoken meaning beneath dialogue.
flashcards.example: 'I'm fine,' she said, turning away. (Subtext: She is definitely not fine, but doesn't want to discuss it.)

flashcards.definition: Engaging all five senses in description — not just what things look like.
flashcards.example: 'The bakery smelled of cinnamon and yeast. Warm air fogged the windows. The crust crackled under her thumb.'

flashcards.definition: Weather/nature reflecting characters' emotions. Use thoughtfully to avoid cliché.
flashcards.example: Storm during emotional conflict. Sunshine at resolution. Subvert: sunshine at a funeral — jarring contrast.

flashcards.definition: The distinctive personality, style, and perspective of the narrator — what makes their telling unique.
flashcards.example: Holden Caulfield's cynical, colloquial voice; Scout Finch's innocent, observant voice.

flashcards.definition: Attribute identifying who is speaking. 'Said' is usually best (invisible to reader).
flashcards.example: 'I can't,' she said. NOT: 'I can't,' she vociferated vehemently. (Overwriting distracts.)

flashcards.definition: A small action replacing a dialogue tag — shows character and anchors speech in scene.
flashcards.example: 'I'm leaving.' He grabbed his keys from the table. (Instead of: 'I'm leaving,' he said angrily.)

flashcards.definition: Using precise, concrete details rather than vague generalisations. Makes writing vivid.
flashcards.example: 'A 1972 mustard-yellow Ford pickup with a dented tailgate' NOT 'an old car.'

flashcards.definition: Imposing artificial limits (word count, banned words, specific form) to spark creativity.
flashcards.example: Write a complete story in exactly 100 words. Write without using the letter 'e.'

flashcards.definition: Be willing to cut writing you love if it doesn't serve the story — editing requires ruthlessness.
flashcards.example: A beautiful paragraph that slows pacing and doesn't advance character or plot — cut it.
